specStatements.text: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.

A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it. A black body does not reflect or transmit any radiation. Since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.
Students should be able to explain:
• that the intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body.

(HT only) A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.
(HT only) The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, reflection of radiation into space.

(HT only) Students should be able to explain how the temperature of a body is related to the balance between incoming radiation absorbed and radiation emitted, using everyday examples to illustrate this balance, and the example of the factors which determine the temperature of the Earth.
(HT only) Students should be able to use information, or draw/interpret diagrams to show how radiation affects the temperature of the Earth’s surface and atmosphere.

scopeNotes.statement: • that the intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks only for an explanation THAT intensity and wavelength distribution depend on temperature. Treatment here is therefore entirely qualitative: a hotter body emits more radiation at every wavelength, and the peak of the distribution shifts towards shorter wavelengths. No radiation law is named or applied - there is no Wien displacement calculation, no Stefan-Boltzmann fourth-power relation, and no numerical work on peak wavelength or emitted power. Students read and compare distribution curves; they are never asked to derive or compute them.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Students should be able to use information, or draw/interpret diagrams to show how radiation affects the temperature of the Earth’s surface and atmosphere.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Earth items stay at the level of an energy-balance diagram: short-wavelength radiation in from the Sun, some reflected straight back to space, the rest absorbed and re-emitted at longer wavelengths, part of which the atmosphere absorbs and radiates back down. Named greenhouse gases, their relative contributions, absorption spectra and any quantitative radiative forcing sit outside this section and are not assessed here.

concepts.definition: Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light. Every object, at any temperature, emits and absorbs it.
The giving out of radiation by an object. All bodies emit radiation, and the hotter the body the more it emits in a given time.
The taking in of radiation incident on an object, so that energy carried by the radiation is transferred to the object.
An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, reflecting none of it and transmitting none of it.
A surface that absorbs radiation well also emits it well, so a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.
How much radiation a body emits per second. It increases as the temperature of the body increases.
How the emitted radiation is spread across a range of wavelengths. Its shape depends on the temperature of the body.
The wavelength at which a body emits most intensely. As a body gets hotter, the peak moves towards shorter wavelengths.
HT only. A body whose temperature is not changing is absorbing radiation at exactly the same rate as it is emitting radiation.
HT only. Absorbing radiation faster than it is emitted. The temperature of the body rises while this is happening.
HT only. Radiation turned back rather than absorbed. Radiation reflected into space never warms the Earth.
HT only. Set by many factors, including the rates at which radiation is absorbed and emitted and reflection of radiation into space.

misconceptions.question: Which objects emit infrared radiation?
misconceptions.correct: All objects emit infrared radiation, whatever their temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Only objects that are hot enough to glow emit infrared radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday examples students meet - a fire, a grill, a filament lamp - are all glowing, so emission gets tied to visible heat.
misconceptions.correction: Emission happens at every temperature. An ice cube emits infrared radiation too, just far less of it each second.

misconceptions.question: Does a body colder than its surroundings emit radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It emits all the time; it simply absorbs more than it emits.
misconceptions.misconception: A body only emits radiation if it is hotter than its surroundings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The temperature-difference rule that governs conduction and net energy transfer is carried over onto the act of emission itself.
misconceptions.correction: Every body emits according to its own temperature. The temperature difference decides the NET transfer, not whether emission happens.

misconceptions.question: Do shiny silver surfaces emit radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, but they are poor emitters compared with dull black surfaces.
misconceptions.misconception: Only dull black surfaces emit radiation; shiny surfaces emit none at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practicals comparing the faces of a Leslie cube show a large difference, which students read as 'emits' versus 'does not emit'.
misconceptions.correction: All surfaces emit. Colour and finish change how good an emitter a surface is, not whether it emits at all.

misconceptions.question: Does a very cold object emit radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, all bodies emit radiation no matter how cold they are.
misconceptions.misconception: Cold objects only absorb radiation; emission starts once they are warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cold is treated as an absence of energy, so a cold object is imagined to have nothing to give out.
misconceptions.correction: There is no threshold temperature for emission. A colder body emits less each second, but it never stops emitting.

misconceptions.question: What happens to radiation incident on a perfect black body?
misconceptions.correct: All of it is absorbed; none is reflected and none is transmitted.
misconceptions.misconception: A perfect black body absorbs most radiation but still reflects or transmits a little.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Real black surfaces do reflect slightly, and students generalise from the imperfect objects in front of them.
misconceptions.correction: 'Perfect' is the whole point of the model: absorption is total, with zero reflection and zero transmission.

misconceptions.question: Is a perfect black body a good emitter or a poor emitter?
misconceptions.correct: The best possible emitter, because a good absorber is also a good emitter.
misconceptions.misconception: A perfect black body keeps hold of the radiation it absorbs, so it emits poorly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption is pictured as trapping or storing, which makes emission sound like the opposite of absorption.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption and emission go together. The surface that absorbs best at a given wavelength also emits best at it.

misconceptions.question: How does the peak wavelength change as a body gets hotter?
misconceptions.correct: The peak of the distribution moves towards shorter wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: The peak moves towards longer wavelengths as the body gets hotter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hotter is associated with 'more' of everything, and students read 'more' as a bigger wavelength number.
misconceptions.correction: Hotter bodies emit more of their radiation at short wavelengths - a filament goes from dull red to blue-white as it heats.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the intensity at each wavelength as a body is heated?
misconceptions.correct: The intensity rises at every wavelength, and the peak shifts as well.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating only shifts the peak; the total radiation emitted stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Attention fixes on the peak because it is the most obvious feature of the curve, so the rise in height is missed.
misconceptions.correction: Both change together: the whole curve rises and its peak moves to shorter wavelengths.

misconceptions.question: What is happening to a body held at constant temperature?
misconceptions.correct: It absorbs and emits radiation at exactly the same rate.
misconceptions.misconception: A body at constant temperature has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nothing is changing' is read as 'nothing is happening', so a dynamic balance is mistaken for no activity at all.
misconceptions.correction: Both processes continue at full rate. They are equal, so there is no net transfer and the temperature holds steady.

misconceptions.question: When does the temperature of a body rise?
misconceptions.correct: When it absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: The temperature rises whenever a body absorbs any radiation at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption alone is linked to warming, and the emission going on at the same time is left out of the account.
misconceptions.correction: It is the balance that matters. A body absorbing radiation can still cool if it emits even faster than it absorbs.

misconceptions.question: What determines the temperature of the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: Many factors, including rates of absorption and emission and reflection.
misconceptions.misconception: The temperature of the Earth is set only by its distance from the Sun.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Distance is the one factor that is easy to picture, and it does control how much radiation arrives.
misconceptions.correction: Arriving radiation is only the start. What is reflected away, what is absorbed and what is emitted all matter.

misconceptions.question: Why does the ground cool less on a cloudy night?
misconceptions.correct: Cloud absorbs radiation from the ground and radiates some of it back down.
misconceptions.misconception: Cloud works like a blanket, trapping warm air and stopping conduction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Blanket' is used loosely in everyday talk about cloud cover, and insulation is a far more familiar idea than radiation.
misconceptions.correction: The mechanism is radiative: the ground still emits, but it also absorbs radiation coming back down from the cloud.

misconceptions.question: Why is radiation leaving the Earth's surface longer in wavelength than radiation arriving from the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: The Earth's surface is far cooler than the Sun, so it emits longer waves.
misconceptions.misconception: The radiation loses energy as it travels up through the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Waves are imagined to tire out over distance, so a change of wavelength gets explained by the journey.
misconceptions.correction: Wavelength is set by the temperature of the emitter. The cool surface emits infrared; the very hot Sun emits much shorter waves.

misconceptions.question: What happens to radiation reflected by clouds and ice?
misconceptions.correct: It returns to space without ever warming the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Reflected radiation is absorbed first, so it still warms the Earth a little.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reflection and absorption both happen 'at the surface', so students blur the two together into one process.
misconceptions.correction: Reflected radiation is turned back before any energy is transferred, which is why bright surfaces keep the Earth cooler.

misconceptions.question: Two identical objects are at different temperatures. Do they emit the same radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The hotter one emits more radiation in a given time.
misconceptions.misconception: What a body emits is fixed by what it is made of, not by its temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emitter quality really does depend on surface and material, so students extend that to mean temperature makes no difference.
misconceptions.correction: Material fixes how good an emitter a surface is; temperature fixes how much it emits and at which wavelengths.

misconceptions.question: Can a body absorb and emit radiation at the same moment?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Absorption and emission go on together, all the time.
misconceptions.misconception: A body does one or the other: while it is absorbing radiation it is not emitting any.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words describe opposite directions of transfer, so they get treated as alternatives that cannot both be happening.
misconceptions.correction: They run simultaneously and independently. It is the difference between the two rates that changes the temperature.

options.text: All objects do, whatever their temperature happens to be
options.rationale: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation.

options.text: Only objects hot enough to glow red, orange or white
options.rationale: Ties emission to visible glow, the only emitters most students have watched.

options.text: Only objects that are warmer than the air near them
options.rationale: Applies the temperature-difference rule for net transfer to emission itself.

options.text: Only objects that have a dull, matt black surface
options.rationale: Confuses being the best emitter with being the only emitter.

mcqs.stem: Two identical iron blocks are held at 30 °C and at 80 °C in the same room. Which statement about the infrared radiation they emit is correct?

options.text: Neither block emits until it is hotter than the room air
options.rationale: Makes emission conditional on being hotter than the surroundings.

options.text: The 80 °C block emits more radiation in a given time
options.rationale: The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.

options.text: Both emit equally, since the blocks are identical
options.rationale: Reads 'identical' as fixing the emission and ignores the temperature difference.

options.text: Only the 80 °C block emits any radiation at all
options.rationale: Treats the cooler block as too cold to emit anything at all.

mcqs.stem: What happens to radiation that is incident on a perfect black body?

options.text: Most is absorbed, but a small part is reflected
options.rationale: Generalises from real black surfaces, which do reflect a little.

options.text: It is all absorbed and stays trapped in the body
options.rationale: m06 holds a black body keeps absorbed radiation, emitting it poorly.

options.text: All of the radiation is absorbed by the body
options.rationale: A perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, reflecting and transmitting none.

options.text: Some is absorbed, the rest passes through
options.rationale: Allows transmission, which a perfect black body does not permit.

mcqs.stem: A perfect black body would be the best possible emitter of radiation. Why?

options.text: It stores the radiation it absorbs and lets it out later
options.rationale: Pictures absorption as storage rather than as the partner of emission.

options.text: Its surface is black, and black surfaces look hottest
options.rationale: Rests the argument on colour alone rather than on absorber-emitter behaviour.

options.text: It reflects and transmits only a tiny amount
options.rationale: m05 holds a black body still reflects and transmits a little, making it near-best.

options.text: A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter
options.rationale: Since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.

mcqs.stem: An ice cube at −15 °C is put on a plate in a warm room. Which statement about the ice cube is correct?

options.text: It absorbs radiation but is much too cold to emit
options.rationale: Assumes a threshold temperature below which a body cannot emit.

options.text: It emits radiation, but it absorbs more than it emits
options.rationale: All bodies emit radiation; the cube is colder than the room, so absorption outweighs emission.

options.text: It only absorbs, because the room around it is warm
options.rationale: Makes emission depend on the temperature difference rather than the cube's own temperature.

options.text: It emits no radiation until it warms up to 0 °C
options.rationale: Invents a melting-point threshold for emission.

mcqs.stem: A lamp filament is heated from dull red to bright white. How does the radiation it emits change?

options.text: Only the intensity rises; the wavelength range is unchanged
options.rationale: Keeps the distribution fixed and changes only its height.

options.text: Only the peak shifts; the intensity stays the same
options.rationale: Notices the colour change but misses the rise in emission.

options.text: The intensity rises and the peak moves to shorter waves
options.rationale: Both the intensity and the wavelength distribution of the emission depend on the temperature of the body.

options.text: The intensity rises and the peak moves to longer waves
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the peak shift the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: Two stars are the same size. Star A looks blue-white and star B looks red. What can be concluded?

options.text: Star B is hotter, since red light carries more energy
options.rationale: Links red to greater energy, reversing the peak-shift rule.

options.text: Star A is cooler, as blue light has a shorter wavelength
options.rationale: Applies m07 (shorter wavelength = cooler) to blue's genuinely shorter wavelength.

options.text: They are equally hot but made of different gases
options.rationale: Attributes the colour to composition and denies any temperature difference.

options.text: Star A is hotter, and its peak wavelength is shorter
options.rationale: The wavelength distribution depends on temperature: the hotter star peaks at shorter wavelengths.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A metal plate inside a hot oven has reached a constant temperature. What does this tell you about the radiation?

options.text: It absorbs radiation as fast as it emits it
options.rationale: A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation.

options.text: It has stopped absorbing and emitting any radiation
options.rationale: Reads 'no change' as 'nothing happening' instead of as a balance.

options.text: It still absorbs radiation but no longer emits any
options.rationale: Keeps absorption running while switching emission off.

options.text: No radiation is absorbed or emitted now
options.rationale: m09 assumes constant temperature means both processes have stopped.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) The temperature of a body is rising. Which statement must be true?

options.text: It absorbs and emits radiation at the same rate
options.rationale: Describes a body at constant temperature, not a rising one.

options.text: It is absorbing radiation and emitting none at all
options.rationale: Assumes warming requires emission to stop completely.

options.text: It is absorbing radiation faster than it emits radiation
options.rationale: The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.

options.text: It is absorbing radiation, and emission cannot cool it
options.rationale: m10 holds absorption alone warms, so emission is treated as irrelevant.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Which factors does the temperature of the Earth depend on?

options.text: Only how close the Earth sits to the Sun in space
options.rationale: m11 sets Earth's temperature solely by its distance from the Sun.

options.text: Only the distance of the Earth from the Sun and its orbit
options.rationale: Stops at the one factor that is easiest to picture.

options.text: Only how much radiation the Earth takes in from the Sun
options.rationale: Counts the incoming side alone and leaves out emission and reflection.

options.text: The rates of absorption and emission, and reflection to space
options.rationale: The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including the rates of absorption and emission of radiation and reflection of radiation into space.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) The ground cools quickly on a clear night, but much less on a cloudy night. Why?

options.text: Cloud radiates energy back down, so the net loss is smaller
options.rationale: The ground still emits, but it now absorbs radiation from the cloud as well, so the imbalance is smaller.

options.text: Cloud acts as an insulating layer, stopping conduction of heat
options.rationale: Swaps the radiative mechanism for an insulation one.

options.text: Cloud completely stops the ground emitting radiation upwards
options.rationale: Switches emission off rather than balancing it against absorption.

options.text: Without cloud, the warm air is not trapped near the ground
options.rationale: m12 treats cloud as a blanket trapping warm air near the surface.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) An energy-balance diagram shows short-wavelength radiation arriving from the Sun and long-wavelength radiation leaving the Earth's surface. Why is the outgoing radiation longer in wavelength?

options.text: The radiation loses energy as it travels up through the air
options.rationale: Explains the change by the journey rather than by the emitter.

options.text: The surface of the Earth is far cooler than the Sun
options.rationale: The wavelength distribution depends on the temperature of the body, and the surface is far cooler than the Sun.

options.text: The atmosphere stretches the waves as they pass through
options.rationale: Invents a stretching mechanism in the atmosphere.

options.text: Only long waves can escape into space from the ground
options.rationale: Makes wavelength a condition for escape instead of a result of temperature.
